verdicts.trueWording: there exists only a single, indisputable answer
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: excluding facts on which sources disagree
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arXiv:2411.04368v1. Abstract carries the quotation word for word; Sec. 2.1 'Must have a single answer' repeats it. But the paper's stated exclusion mechanism is annotator-based, not source-based: Sec. 2.2 removes a question when two AI trainers' answers disagree per a ChatGPT classifier, or when the second trainer judged it not timeless / lacking an indisputable answer. 'Sources disagree' is the claimant's gloss; the paper never frames exclusion that way (it only requires two unique source domains across the trainers).

verdicts.trueWording: each hallucinate between 17% and 33% of the time
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arXiv:2405.20362v1, Abstract, word for word. Every limb holds: the abstract names LexisNexis (Lexis+ AI) and Thomson Reuters (Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, Ask Practical Law AI), and 'retrieval-grounded' is the paper's own framing (RAG touted by providers; contribution 1 assesses 'RAG-based proprietary legal AI tools').

Raw PDF arXiv:2405.20362v1, Section 1 Introduction (p.4 of the preprint), word for word in the sentence beginning 'LexisNexis's Lexis+ AI is the highest-performing system we test'. The 'highest performing system tested' limb is stated on the page. A results figure later restates 65% for Lexis+ AI.

verdicts.trueWording: Westlaw's AI-Assisted Research is accurate 42% of the time
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arXiv:2405.20362v1, Section 1 Introduction, word for word (source uses a curly apostrophe in Westlaw's). Same evaluation as index 1266 — the sentence sits in the same paragraph. Page adds that Westlaw hallucinates nearly twice as often as the other legal tools.

verdicts.trueWording: they provided incorrect answers to more than 60 percent of queries
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched live from cjr.org with a browser user agent (HTTP 200), section 'Chatbots' responses to our queries were often confidently wrong'. Quotation word for word. Every limb supported by the Methodology section: eight generative search tools; excerpts supplied; 'we asked it to identify the corresponding article's headline, original publisher, publication date, and URL'.

verdicts.trueWording: with Perplexity answering 37 percent of the queries incorrectly
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that 37% and 94% are the range endpoints across all eight tools
verdicts.note: Raw cjr.org page carries both figures word for word ('while Grok 3 had a much higher error rate, answering 94 percent of the queries incorrectly'), but never says these are the lowest and highest. Per-tool rates for the other six appear only in chart images, and the article separately notes Copilot 'declined more questions than it answered', so a lower incorrect rate than Perplexity's 37% is not excluded. The two numbers are right; 'ranged from ... to' is the claimant's inference.

verdicts.trueWording: cited fabricated or broken URLs that led to error pages
verdicts.note: Raw cjr.org page, word for word in 'More than half of responses from Gemini and Grok 3 cited fabricated or broken URLs that led to error pages.' The following sentences add that 154 of 200 Grok 3 citations led to error pages.

verdicts.trueWording: RS scores barely approaching 30, while most LLMs score below 15
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arXiv:2604.24690v1 (paper exists; downloaded and text-extracted, 14 pp.). Section 5.2 'Main results', word for word across a line break, in 'even top-performing LLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro and Qwen3-235B achieve RS scores barely approaching 30, while most LLMs score below 15.' Table 4 is consistent (top RS 28.14; majority under 15).

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the highest of the closed-source models listed
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arXiv:2604.24690v1, Table 4 (p.6): the row is exact, so RS 26.71 for Gemini-3-Pro-Preview is confirmed. The superlative is refuted by the same table: the Closed-Source block also lists Gemini-3-Pro-Preview-Thinking at RS 26.73, higher than 26.71. Highest closed-source RS in Table 4 is 26.73, not 26.71.

verdicts.trueWording: only Claude used em dashes more than professional writers
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext via en.wikipedia Special:Export. Section Style > 'Overuse of em dashes' (nesting confirmed: ==Style== precedes ===Overuse of em dashes===). Final sentence of that section reads 'A July 2026 study found that of contemporary models only Claude used em dashes more than professional writers, and ChatGPT used them less.' The attached ref is exactly the cited relay: {{cite web |title=How to spot AI writing |website=The Economist |date=30 July 2026}}. Verified only that the Wikipedia page relays this, which is what the claim asserts; the Economist study itself was not opened.

Raw PDF arXiv:2301.07597, Section 3 'Major Differences between Human and ChatGPT', item (c), word for word, immediately after 'Humans also love to apply humor, irony, metaphors, and examples'. Attribution nuance worth noting but not a failed limb: Sec. 3.2 'Human Summarization' says the list distils 200+ feedbacks from 17 volunteer testers 'combined with our observations' — the paper says volunteers, not annotators.

verdicts.trueWording: present participial clauses at 2 to 5 times the rate
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arXiv:2503.02879v2 = Huang, Xu, Geng, Wan, Chen, 'Wikipedia in the Era of LLMs', Transactions on Machine Learning Research 02/2026 — matches the cited venue and date. Section 4.2 'Direct Impact 2: Linguistic Style', Sentence Level paragraph: 'Reinhart et al. (2025) revealed that LLMs use present participial clauses at 2 to 5 times the rate of human text while using the passive voice at roughly half the rate as human texts.' Both limbs and the relaying attribution hold.

verdicts.trueWording: 13 times more likely to contain a “blacklisted” source
verdicts.note: Raw PDF arXiv:2511.09685 (Triedman & Mantzarlis, Cornell Tech), p.1 summary of findings: 'Non-CC-licensed articles on Grokipedia are 3.2 times more likely than the same articles on Wikipedia to contain a citation that the English Wikipedia community has deemed “generally unreliable” and 13 times more likely to contain a “blacklisted” source.' Every limb — non-CC-licensed subset, same-article comparison, English Wikipedia's blacklist — is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: heading 'G15. LLM-generated pages without human review'; 'reasonable human review' required
verdicts.note: Claim carried no quote, so VERIFIED_SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM. Raw wikitext via Special:Export. The page opens with {{proposal}} (standing proposal) and the heading 'G15. LLM-generated pages without human review'; its body requires that the page 'could only plausibly have been generated by large language models (LLM) and would have been removed by any reasonable human review', with a footnote defining reasonable human review. 'Earlier wording' checked against the live policy: WP:Speedy deletion now heads the criterion 'G15. Unambiguously LLM-generated pages', keeps the old title only as an anchor, and has dropped the reasonable-human-review clause after a 2026 RfC. Page creator confirmed via the MediaWiki API: first revision by user Ca, 2026-06-06, comment 'rough draft'.

verdicts.trueWording: des références bibliographiques plausibles mais fictives
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext via fr.wikipedia Special:Exporter. Section 'Les sources : principal critère de vérification' > 'Types de problèmes rencontrés' opens 'Les contenus générés par IA présentent fréquemment :' and lists, third bullet, the quoted phrase word for word. Page is the Projet:Observatoire des IA report of the 9 May live session, self-described as AI-generated but proofread.
